defaults.permitted_development: Across Essex, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across Essex, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Essex, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: A wraparound only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both work under Class A when taken together. rules.height_rules: For height, the familiar Class A envelope still applies, but the side arm is usually the sensitive part because of the 3m eaves rule close to a boundary. rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
